steps.answer: Maeterlinck's account of swarming describes scout bees, which leave the hanging swarm at its first moment, search in all directions for a lodging, and return one by one to report on what they found (The Swarm: from The Life of the Bee, p. 34 of scan). The passages I read stop there and do not explain how the swarm weighs those reports and settles on one site. This book dates from 1906 and is a literary naturalist's account, so it is out of date on the mechanism; later research on honeybee scouts (such as waggle dancing and collective voting) is not in these sources and should be checked in a modern text. The catalog search for nest-site choice returned no direct hits, so the best next step is a modern book on swarm biology.
